# ![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.38391v1/figure/scope-mascot.png) SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Qirui Liu    Wei Cao    Yu Mi    Yichen Sun    Xuekun Zhang    Lei Liu
   Yue Shen    Zhixuan Chu Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[ Email:
<zhixuanchu@zju.edu.cn>

###### Abstract

Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) improves long-horizon LLM
agents through task-level feedback, but provides limited supervision
over intermediate decisions. Our analysis reveals an _outcome–step
mismatch_: successful trajectories can contain erroneous steps, while
failed trajectories may include correct decisions. To provide
finer-grained guidance, recent methods incorporate hindsight skills into
on-policy self-distillation. However, we further find that applying
trajectory-level skills across all steps can introduce off-target
distillation signals at decisions unrelated to the intended corrections.
Motivated by these observations, we introduce SCOPE, a framework for
_Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation_. SCOPE first
equips the policy with error-localization and skill-generation
capabilities through lightweight supervised initialization. During
online RL, the policy analyzes its own trajectories, generates
step-specific corrective skills, and distills their guidance exclusively
at selected error steps. A bounded signed distillation coefficient
stabilizes auxiliary updates while preserving both reinforcement and
suppression, and a success-relative pairwise length reward encourages
efficient task completion. Experiments across three smaller backbones on
ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements. With
Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% and 85.2% success, outperforming SEED
by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively. On Qwen3-32B, SCOPE
achieves 99.2% ALFWorld success versus 85.2% for GRPO, while reducing
average interactions by 65.0%.

## 1 Introduction

LLM agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls and environment
interactions \[[38](#bib.bib1), [20](#bib.bib2), [12](#bib.bib3)\].
Reinforcement learning (RL) improves these decisions using task feedback
\[[17](#bib.bib4), [28](#bib.bib5), [8](#bib.bib6)\]. In particular,
GRPO \[[22](#bib.bib7)\] converts the outcomes of sampled trajectories
into relative advantages, providing a scalable training signal without
step-level annotations \[[15](#bib.bib8), [30](#bib.bib9),
[28](#bib.bib5)\]. However, an outcome reward reveals whether a task was
completed, with little indication of which intermediate decisions were
sound or required correction.

This distinction matters because trajectory success and step quality do
not always agree. A successful agent may recover from invalid or
mistaken actions, while a failed agent may make useful progress before a
consequential error. We examine this _outcome–step mismatch_ in
annotated WebShop trajectories. Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a)
shows 29.8% erroneous steps in the successful group and 42.4% correct
steps in the failed group. These observations motivate identifying
errors independently of the final outcome. When an outcome-level
advantage is shared across a trajectory, it cannot distinguish these
local differences in decision quality \[[6](#bib.bib10),
[5](#bib.bib11), [10](#bib.bib12)\].

To compensate for coarse outcome feedback, recent methods introduce
hindsight-based supervision to provide additional guidance on agent
decisions. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) \[[42](#bib.bib13)\]
enables such guidance: a teacher branch receives privileged context and
scores actions sampled by the ordinary policy \[[1](#bib.bib14),
[11](#bib.bib15)\]. Trajectory-derived skills summarize useful hindsight
\[[3](#bib.bib16)\], and methods such as SEED train the policy to
generate this guidance from its own experience \[[26](#bib.bib17),
[29](#bib.bib18)\]. However, privileged skill context can induce
off-target probability shifts at steps unrelated to the skill. A
trajectory-level skill may address a particular mistake or subgoal, yet
conditioning the teacher on it throughout the trajectory can also change
token probabilities at other steps. EOPSA \[[11](#bib.bib15)\]
highlights a related issue: privileged prompts can introduce
task-irrelevant discrepancies that dilute useful distillation signals.
In our agentic setting, Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(b)
shows that skill-unrelated steps account for 57.9% of nonzero
sampled-token gaps. Among these off-target signals, 53.9% are negative
and 46.1% are positive. Distilling across all steps assigns auxiliary
updates to these probability shifts even where the skill offers no
correction for the current decision.

Together, these observations raise a central question:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We introduce SCOPE, a framework for _Selective Critical-Step On-Policy
Self-Distillation_. A lightweight supervised warm-up teaches the policy
to locate errors and generate corrective skills. During online RL, the
policy analyzes its own trajectories to identify critical errors in both
successful and failed episodes and generates corresponding step-specific
skills. A skill-conditioned self-teacher then provides corrective
supervision exclusively at the selected steps, aligning distillation
with the decisions that require correction.

During training, however, we observe occasional abrupt performance
collapses with unbounded OPSD updates, as illustrated in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c).
Large teacher–student log-probability gaps can amplify auxiliary updates
and destabilize optimization. To mitigate this instability, SCOPE
employs a _bounded signed_ distillation coefficient that limits extreme
updates while preserving both reinforcement and suppression. Moreover,
successful trajectories may still contain redundant interactions,
motivating a success-relative pairwise length reward to encourage
efficient task completion. Together, these designs enable stable,
targeted, and efficiency-aware agentic RL.

Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three backbones demonstrate
consistent improvements. With Qwen2.5-3B, SCOPE achieves 97.7% and 85.2%
success, outperforming SEED by 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points,
respectively. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE achieves 89.6% success
(+23.2 points) with 46.7% fewer interactions. Extending to Qwen3-32B,
SCOPE reaches 99.2% ALFWorld success (+14.0 points over GRPO) with 65.0%
fewer interactions.

In summary, our contributions are fourfold:

- •
  We reveal two limitations of trajectory-level supervision in agentic
  RL: outcome–step mismatch, where trajectory success does not reliably
  reflect individual decision quality, and off-target distillation
  signals induced by privileged skills at unrelated steps.
- •
  We propose SCOPE, a selective on-policy self-distillation framework
  that bootstraps critical-step analysis from supervised warm-up,
  generates step-specific corrective skills from online trajectories,
  and distills their guidance exclusively at identified error steps.
- •
  We introduce a bounded signed distillation coefficient to mitigate
  unstable auxiliary updates while preserving both positive and negative
  corrections, together with a success-relative pairwise length reward
  to encourage efficient task completion.
- •
  We validate SCOPE on ALFWorld and WebShop across three backbones and
  further extend it to Qwen3-32B. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE
  improves success by 23.2 points with 46.7% fewer interactions. With
  Qwen3-32B, it achieves 99.2% seen and 94.0% unseen ALFWorld success.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents

Reinforcement learning trains LLM agents through feedback from tool use
and environment interaction \[[31](#bib.bib19), [14](#bib.bib20),
[33](#bib.bib21)\]. ToolRL \[[17](#bib.bib4)\], RAGEN
\[[28](#bib.bib5)\], and Search-R1 \[[8](#bib.bib6)\] apply this
approach to tool selection, interactive planning, and information
seeking. GRPO \[[22](#bib.bib7)\] provides a common optimization
backbone by comparing trajectory outcomes within a sampled group.
However, trajectory-level advantages offer limited resolution over
intermediate decisions in long interactions. GiGPO \[[6](#bib.bib10)\]
estimates step-level advantages through hierarchical grouping, while
GraphGPO \[[5](#bib.bib11)\] leverages state-transition graphs to refine
credit assignment. Rather than directly re-estimating step-level RL
advantages, SCOPE complements outcome-based RL with hindsight error
localization and targeted corrective distillation.

### 2.2 Hindsight Skills for LLM Agents

Experience can guide agents through verbal reflection, reusable skills,
or explicit memory, as demonstrated by Reflexion \[[23](#bib.bib22)\],
Voyager \[[25](#bib.bib23)\], and ExpeL \[[41](#bib.bib24)\]. Recent
methods further internalize such guidance through policy training
\[[16](#bib.bib25), [36](#bib.bib26), [26](#bib.bib17),
[27](#bib.bib27)\]. SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\] retrieves skills from an
external skill bank to provide privileged teacher context, while
Skill-SD \[[26](#bib.bib17)\] derives teacher-only skills from completed
agent trajectories. OPID \[[36](#bib.bib26)\] constructs hierarchical
episode- and step-level skills through critical-first routing, falling
back to episode-level guidance at non-critical steps.

SEED \[[29](#bib.bib18)\] introduces a policy-synchronized hindsight
analyzer. After a supervised warm-up, the policy acts as both actor and
analyzer, generating trajectory-level skills that evolve with online
training. However, conditioning distillation on such skills across all
steps can introduce off-target signals at unrelated decisions. GRSD
\[[43](#bib.bib29)\] contrasts policy-generated reflections from
successful and failed trajectories to construct group-level guidance for
turn-level credit assignment. In contrast, SCOPE internalizes
critical-step analysis, generates step-specific corrective skills, and
restricts their supervision to identified errors in both successful and
failed trajectories.

### 2.3 On-Policy Self-Distillation

Knowledge distillation transfers teacher guidance to a student model
\[[7](#bib.bib30), [9](#bib.bib31)\]. On-policy distillation instead
evaluates student-generated sequences, reducing the distribution
mismatch associated with offline demonstrations \[[19](#bib.bib32),
[1](#bib.bib14)\]. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) constructs a
teacher from the same model under privileged context \[[42](#bib.bib13),
[11](#bib.bib15)\]. RLSD \[[35](#bib.bib33)\] uses teacher–student
discrepancies to modulate token-level update magnitudes while retaining
reward-determined optimization directions. SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\]
employs a sigmoid gate that emphasizes positive teacher endorsements
while attenuating negative rejections, improving auxiliary training
stability. AgentOPSD \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] aggregates token-level
discrepancies and recursively updates belief states for turn-level
credit assignment. SOD \[[44](#bib.bib34)\] adaptively weights
step-level distillation according to teacher–student divergence.

However, teacher–student discrepancies do not necessarily reflect
task-relevant corrections. EOPSA \[[11](#bib.bib15)\] highlights how
privileged prompting can introduce task-irrelevant stylistic shifts that
dilute useful distillation signals. In agentic tasks, skill conditioning
may similarly affect decisions unrelated to the intended correction.
Unlike divergence-based weighting, SCOPE identifies critical errors
through self-generated hindsight analysis and restricts auxiliary
distillation to these steps. A bounded signed coefficient further limits
extreme teacher–student updates while preserving both positive and
negative corrections.

## 3 Method

![Refer to caption](2610.38391v1/method-v1.png)

Figure 2: Overview of SCOPE. Supervised initialization teaches the
policy to analyze trajectories and generate corrective skills. During
online training, the policy collects and analyzes its own rollouts,
assigns skills to selected error steps, and combines selective
self-distillation with efficiency-aware GRPO.

SCOPE supplements outcome-based RL with corrective supervision at
selected error steps (Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")).
A supervised warm-up teaches the policy to locate mistakes and generate
corrective skills. During online training, the same policy analyzes its
rollouts, and a skill-conditioned self-teacher scores the sampled
actions at the selected steps. Bounded signed self-distillation
transfers these corrections to the student, while a success-relative
length reward encourages efficient task completion.

### 3.1 Agent Interaction and Policy Snapshots

For a task $`q`$, the agent receives observation $`o_{t}`$ and generates
a response $`a_{t}=(y_{t,1},\ldots,y_{t,L_{t}})`$ from its available
interaction history $`h_{t}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
h_{t}=(q,o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}).
``` |  | (1) |

The response contains the model-generated reasoning and action tokens
for one environment interaction. The environment executes the action and
returns $`o_{t+1}`$. A completed trajectory
$`\tau_{i}=\{(h_{i,t},a_{i,t},o_{i,t+1})\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}}`$ contains
$`T_{i}`$ interaction steps and receives a task reward $`R_{i}`$. We
denote its binary success indicator by $`z_{i}\in\{0,1\}`$, where
$`z_{i}=1`$ indicates successful task completion. Interaction length
$`T_{i}`$ and response-token length $`L_{i,t}`$ are distinct quantities.

At outer iteration $`u`$, we take a policy snapshot
$`\bar{\theta}_{u}=\theta_{u}`$ and sample $`N`$ trajectories for each
task:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}_{q}^{(u)}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\qquad\tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{u}}(\cdot\mid q).
``` |  | (2) |

This snapshot supplies the actor, the hindsight analyzer, and the
privileged teacher used to construct the update data. The trainable
student starts from this checkpoint and updates its parameters
$`\theta`$ across successive minibatches, while $`\bar{\theta}_{u}`$
remains fixed for the current outer iteration.

### 3.2 Self-Bootstrapped Error Analysis

#### Supervised initialization

We first train the policy to analyze trajectories through supervised
fine-tuning, following SEED \[[29](#bib.bib18)\]. GLM-5.2
\[[40](#bib.bib35)\] labels errors in a small pool of base-policy
trajectories and writes a short corrective skill for each error or group
of related errors. A skill entry is represented as
$`(\mathcal{D}_{i,k},s_{i,k},e_{i,k})`$, where $`\mathcal{D}_{i,k}`$ is
a nonempty set of target-step indices, $`s_{i,k}`$ is the corrective
skill, and $`e_{i,k}`$ contains the error explanation and supporting
evidence. A singleton target set describes one mistake; several steps
may share a skill when they require the same correction.

Let $`x_{i}`$ be the serialized analysis input and $`Y_{i}`$ its
structured annotation. The warm-up minimizes the autoregressive
objective

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x_{i},Y_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}\left[\sum_{r=1}^{|Y_{i}|}\log\pi_{\theta}(Y_{i,r}\mid x_{i},Y_{i,<r})\right],
``` |  | (3) |

where $`Y_{i,r}`$ is an annotation token. The resulting checkpoint
initializes online training. External annotation is confined to this
offline stage. Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
describes data preparation, and Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C SFT and Analyzer Prompt Templates ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
gives the SFT and analyzer prompt templates.

#### Online hindsight analysis

The analyzer inspects successful and failed trajectories separately. For
a successful trajectory, it uses the trajectory’s own observations,
responses, and action-validity feedback to identify avoidable mistakes.
For a failed trajectory, it additionally receives the action sequences
of successful trajectories from the same on-policy task group. With
$`\operatorname{Act}(\tau)`$ denoting an extracted action sequence, the
reference context is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{i}=\begin{cases}\{\operatorname{Act}(\tau_{j}):\tau_{j}\in\mathcal{G}_{q}^{(u)},\ z_{j}=1\},&z_{i}=0,\\
\varnothing,&z_{i}=1.\end{cases}
``` |  | (4) |

Successful references demonstrate feasible task progress. The analyzer
judges each decision using the information available at that step and
the resulting environmental feedback, allowing valid alternative
strategies and reasonable exploration.

The policy snapshot generates the analysis under an analysis-specific
prompt:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{Y}_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{A}_{\bar{\theta}_{u}}(\cdot\mid\tau_{i},\mathcal{R}_{i}),`$ |  | (5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{Y}_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{(\mathcal{D}_{i,k},\widehat{s}_{i,k},\widehat{e}_{i,k})\}_{k=1}^{J_{i}},\qquad J_{i}\leq K_{\max}.`$ |  |  |

The limit $`K_{\max}`$ bounds the number of skill entries, not the total
number of selected steps. Parsing removes nonexistent target indices and
duplicate assignments, so the retained target sets are disjoint. The
selected-step set is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{i}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{J_{i}}\mathcal{D}_{i,k},\qquad m_{i,t}=\mathbb{I}[t\in\mathcal{C}_{i}].
``` |  | (6) |

Each selected step receives the skill of its assigned entry, denoted
$`\widehat{s}_{i,t}`$. The analyzer may return an empty set when no
clear error is supported, including when a failed group supplies no
successful reference. An unselected step receives no auxiliary
distillation signal.

At the next outer iteration, the updated policy supplies both the actor
and analyzer.

### 3.3 Bounded Signed Self-Distillation

#### Step-specific teacher guidance

We use skill-conditioned on-policy self-distillation to transfer
hindsight guidance into the ordinary policy \[[26](#bib.bib17),
[36](#bib.bib26)\]. For each selected step, a context augmentation
function $`H`$ inserts its assigned skill into the ordinary policy
input: $`\widetilde{h}_{i,t}=H(h_{i,t},\widehat{s}_{i,t})`$. We retain
the original sampled response and its within-response prefix. Teacher
and student score the same token, using parameters
$`\vartheta_{T}=\bar{\theta}_{u}`$ and $`\vartheta_{S}=\theta`$ and
contexts $`h^{T}_{i,t}=\widetilde{h}_{i,t}`$ and
$`h^{S}_{i,t}=h_{i,t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell^{b}_{i,t,\ell}=\log\pi_{\vartheta_{b}}(y_{i,t,\ell}\mid h^{b}_{i,t},y_{i,t,<\ell}),\quad b\in\{T,S\}.
``` |  | (7) |

Teacher log-probabilities are computed once before actor optimization
and cached for the selected steps. Student log-probabilities are
recomputed at each training forward pass as $`\theta`$ changes.

#### Bounding the signed learning signal

Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Bounding the signed learning signal ‣ 3.3 Bounded Signed Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
shows an anomaly during minibatch optimization. At outer update 26, the
pre-optimization gap is 0.284 nats. During training, the student’s mean
sampled-token log-probability drops to $`-2716.0`$ nats, while the
cached teacher mean remains at $`-0.440`$ nats. The training-stage gap
reaches 2715.5 nats, with a non-finite recorded gradient norm.

Teacher scores are cached before actor optimization. Successive
minibatch updates change $`\theta`$, so training forwards compare
updated student scores with the fixed teacher cache. A sharp drop in
student probabilities on sampled tokens can therefore turn a moderate
pre-optimization gap into an extreme training-stage discrepancy. In our
training runs, the observed instability arises from the raw-gap OPSD
auxiliary loss rather than the GRPO objective: the discrepancy directly
scales the student’s score gradient and can amplify auxiliary updates.

Figure 3: Anomaly during minibatch optimization. (a) Pre-optimization
and training-stage gaps (symmetric-log axis). (b) Current student and
cached teacher sampled-token log-probabilities. Dashed lines mark outer
update 26.

We control gap-driven amplification by replacing the raw gap with a
bounded signed coefficient:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{i,t,\ell}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{sg}[\ell^{T}_{i,t,\ell}-\ell^{S}_{i,t,\ell}(\theta)],`$ |  | (8) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{dist}}_{i,t,\ell}`$ | $`\displaystyle=c\,\tanh\!\left(\frac{\alpha\Delta_{i,t,\ell}}{c}\right),`$ |  |  |

where $`\operatorname{sg}`$ stops gradients through the coefficient. The
parameters $`\alpha>0`$ and $`c>0`$ control the slope at zero and
saturation magnitude: $`\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{dist}}\approx\alpha\Delta`$
for small gaps, and $`|\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{dist}}|<c`$ for finite gaps.
This symmetric transformation preserves the gap’s sign and gives zero
guidance when teacher and student agree on the sampled token.

We optimize a sampled-token surrogate rather than a full-distribution
KL, using tokens from the sampled responses. Let $`\mathcal{T}`$ denote
the valid, retained response-token positions in the current training
microbatch, and let $`\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sel}}`$ contain only those
positions belonging to selected error steps. Writing
$`N_{\mathrm{sel}}=|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sel}}|`$, the distillation loss
is simply the mean over these selected tokens:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\frac{c}{N_{\mathrm{sel}}}\sum_{(i,t,\ell)\in\mathcal{T}}m_{i,t}\cdot\tanh\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{c}\operatorname{sg}[\ell^{T}_{i,t,\ell}-\ell^{S}_{i,t,\ell}(\theta)]\right)\ell^{S}_{i,t,\ell}(\theta).`$ |  | (9) |

Unselected steps do not enter this loss or its token count. If
$`N_{\mathrm{sel}}=0`$, we set $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}=0`$.

For each selected token, the contribution to the policy gradient is
$`-\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{dist}}\nabla_{\theta}\ell^{S}/N_{\mathrm{sel}}`$.
The derivative with respect to its student log-probability has magnitude
at most $`c/N_{\mathrm{sel}}`$. With $`c=1`$, the coefficient is
confined to $`[-1,1]`$, controlling the influence of extreme
teacher–student discrepancies on distillation updates. The signed
transformation reinforces positive-gap tokens and suppresses
negative-gap tokens, retaining corrective guidance in both directions.

SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\] also addresses OPSD instability with a bounded
sigmoid gate. Its nonnegative auxiliary coefficient attenuates teacher
rejections without retaining their suppressive direction. SCOPE
preserves this negative guidance at selected error steps through a
signed coefficient, while bounding both update directions. Appendix
[A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Bounded Signed Distillation ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
derives the fixed-data log-cosh interpretation and auxiliary-gradient
bounds; Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Influence of Irrelevant Selected Tokens ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
bounds the contribution of irrelevant selected tokens.

### 3.4 Success-Relative Pairwise Efficiency

Selective distillation corrects identified errors. Successful
trajectories can also contain redundant interactions. Length-aware
rewards have been explored to balance correctness and computational cost
in reasoning models. L1 \[[2](#bib.bib36)\] combines correctness with
adherence to a specified token-length budget, while ShorterBetter
\[[39](#bib.bib37)\] uses the shortest correct response in a sampled
group as a dynamic length reference. For multi-turn agents, we measure
efficiency by the number of environment interactions and compare
successful trajectories for the same task within the current rollout
group. This provides a policy-relative reference as successful
interaction lengths evolve during training.

Let
$`\mathcal{S}_{q}=\{i:\tau_{i}\in\mathcal{G}_{q}^{(u)},\ z_{i}=1\}`$.
For two distinct successful trajectories, we use a Bradley–Terry
pairwise comparison \[[4](#bib.bib38)\] with utility
$`-\log T_{i}/\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{ij}=\sigma\!\left(\frac{\log T_{j}-\log T_{i}}{\tau_{\mathrm{len}}}\right),
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}`$ and $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}>0`$
controls the smoothness of the preference. The score exceeds $`1/2`$
when trajectory $`i`$ is shorter than trajectory $`j`$. Averaging over
the other successful trajectories gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
b_{i}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{q}|-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{q}\setminus\{i\}}p_{ij},&|\mathcal{S}_{q}|\geq 2,\\[6.0pt]
\frac{1}{2},&|\mathcal{S}_{q}|=1,\end{cases}\quad i\in\mathcal{S}_{q}.
``` |  | (11) |

Each complete trajectory enters this comparison once, regardless of how
many turn records it produces. We add the resulting efficiency bonus to
the original task reward $`R_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}=\begin{cases}R_{i}+\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}b_{i},&z_{i}=1,\\
R_{i},&z_{i}=0.\end{cases}
``` |  | (12) |

Here $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}>0`$ controls the bonus strength, and
length preferences apply only to successes. A lone success receives
$`b_{i}=1/2`$, yielding $`R_{i}+\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}/2`$ without
relative-length information. A group with no successes receives no
efficiency bonus.

The comparison is invariant to a common positive rescaling of all
lengths, because $`\log(aT_{j})-\log(aT_{i})=\log T_{j}-\log T_{i}`$.
The score therefore depends on proportional length differences, without
requiring an absolute target length. Moreover, $`p_{ij}+p_{ji}=1`$, so
the mean $`b_{i}`$ over successes is $`1/2`$. The pairwise term
allocates a bounded efficiency bonus among successful trajectories with
mean bonus $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}/2`$. Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Properties of Success-Relative Efficiency Rewards ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
proves the ordering, scale invariance, and bonus-conservation properties
of this reward.

### 3.5 Joint Policy Optimization

We combine GRPO with selective self-distillation. For each task $`q`$,
we normalize the task-and-length reward $`R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}`$ across
$`N`$ sampled trajectories:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}=\frac{R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}-\mu_{q}}{\sigma_{q}+\epsilon_{A}},
``` |  | (13) |

where $`\mu_{q}`$ and $`\sigma_{q}`$ denote the mean and standard
deviation of the rewards within the task group, and $`\epsilon_{A}>0`$
ensures numerical stability. All steps and tokens in trajectory
$`\tau_{i}`$ share the same advantage $`A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}`$. With the
clipped surrogate from PPO \[[21](#bib.bib39)\], the GRPO objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\big[\min\{\rho A^{\mathrm{RL}},\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A^{\mathrm{RL}}\}\big]`$ |  | (14) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-\lambda_{H}\mathcal{H}_{\theta}.`$ |  |  |

Here $`\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}}`$ averages over retained response
tokens, with $`A^{\mathrm{RL}}=A_{i}^{\mathrm{RL}}`$ for tokens
belonging to trajectory $`i`$; token indices are omitted inside the
expectation. The importance ratio is
$`\rho_{i,t,\ell}(\theta)=\exp(\ell^{S}_{i,t,\ell}(\theta)-\ell^{\mathrm{old}}_{i,t,\ell})`$,
where $`\ell^{\mathrm{old}}`$ is the sampled-token log-probability under
the rollout policy. The parameter $`\epsilon`$ is the clipping radius.
The coefficients $`\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ and $`\lambda_{H}`$ weight the
KL penalty to the fixed reference policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ and the
policy entropy $`\mathcal{H}_{\theta}`$, respectively. The entropy bonus
encourages continued exploration.

We add the selective OPSD loss to the RL objective:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta).
``` |  | (15) |

The coefficient $`\lambda`$ balances outcome-based learning with
corrective supervision at selected error steps. After each outer
iteration, the updated policy serves as actor and analyzer for the next
round.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate SCOPE through six research questions:

- •
  RQ1: Overall Effectiveness. Does SCOPE outperform outcome-based RL and
  skill-guided baselines across tasks and backbones? (Section
  [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
- •
  RQ2: Error Localization. What limitations arise from trajectory-level
  supervision, and can SCOPE reliably identify critical error steps?
  (Sections
  [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Diagnosing Trajectory-Level Supervision ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
  and
  [4.7](#S4.SS7 "4.7 Error-Localization Capability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
- •
  RQ3: Component Contributions. How do supervised initialization,
  selective skill guidance, and pairwise length rewards affect
  performance and efficiency? (Section
  [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
- •
  RQ4: Optimization Behavior. How do training efficiency, stability, and
  hyperparameter choices affect SCOPE? (Sections
  [4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
  and
  [4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Parameter Sensitivity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
- •
  RQ5: Unseen Generalization. Does SCOPE generalize to unseen tasks
  while improving interaction efficiency? (Section
  [4.8](#S4.SS8 "4.8 Generalization to Unseen Tasks ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
- •
  RQ6: Larger-Model Scalability. Can SCOPE maintain its effectiveness
  and interaction efficiency when extended to Qwen3-32B? (Section
  [4.9](#S4.SS9 "4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmarks and metrics

We evaluate SCOPE on ALFWorld and WebShop, following the evaluation
protocols of SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\]. ALFWorld \[[24](#bib.bib40)\]
tests household task completion through text-based interaction. Each
validation round contains 128 episodes from the seen split, covering six
task families: Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, and Pick2. We report
success rates by family and the overall success rate across the 128
episodes (micro-average). WebShop \[[37](#bib.bib41)\] requires agents
to search, inspect, and purchase products satisfying a user’s
requirements. We evaluate on the same fixed set of 128 tasks and report
two metrics: the mean normalized task score, which measures how well the
purchased product meets the requirements, and the success rate, which
counts fully completed tasks. All reported scores are percentages.

#### Backbones and evaluation context

We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \[[18](#bib.bib42)\],
and Qwen3-1.7B \[[34](#bib.bib43)\] to examine performance across model
sizes and generations. Comparisons are made within each backbone. At
evaluation, SCOPE acts from the ordinary interaction history without
hindsight skills or analyzer calls. For the main ALFWorld and WebShop
comparison, we report SCOPE’s validation metrics logged at training step
150. The corresponding single-run validation curves for both Qwen2.5
backbones are provided in Appendix
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Validation Curves Across Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
An asterisk marks a baseline that receives skills at evaluation; the
other baselines use their ordinary policy inputs. Key training settings
and diagnostic protocols are provided in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

#### Baselines

We compare against eight baselines. Vanilla evaluates the original
backbone without additional agentic training. Skill-Prompt\* supplies
retrieved skills in the evaluation prompt without updating the model,
following the prompting baseline in SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\]. GRPO
\[[22](#bib.bib7)\] learns from group-relative task rewards without an
auxiliary distillation objective.

The remaining methods incorporate self-distillation or hindsight
guidance into agentic RL. AgentOPSD \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] aggregates
teacher–student gaps by turn and uses recursive belief updates to assign
turn-level credit. SDAR \[[13](#bib.bib28)\] retrieves teacher guidance
from a skill bank and controls auxiliary self-distillation with bounded
token-level gates. OPID \[[36](#bib.bib26)\] uses an external analyzer
to construct hierarchical skills, retaining episode-level guidance at
non-critical steps. GRSD \[[43](#bib.bib29)\] uses policy-generated
reflections scored by an external judge to construct group-level
guidance and refine turn-level credit assignment. SEED
\[[29](#bib.bib18)\] initializes hindsight analysis through SFT and
iteratively uses the updated policy to generate and distill
trajectory-level skills.

### 4.2 Main Results

Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
compares SCOPE with eight baselines across three backbones, grouped by
their auxiliary guidance types. SCOPE achieves the highest WebShop
success across all backbones and the highest or tied highest ALFWorld
success.

#### Beyond outcome-level supervision

Compared with GRPO, SCOPE improves ALFWorld success by 22.7, 17.2, and
46.1 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen3-1.7B,
respectively. The corresponding WebShop gains are 21.9, 11.8, and 40.6
points. These consistent improvements suggest the benefit of
complementing coarse outcome rewards with localized corrective
supervision, rather than relying solely on trajectory-level feedback.

#### Self-bootstrapped error analysis versus external supervision

OPID relies on an external analyzer to identify critical steps and
generate hierarchical skills, while GRSD uses an external judge to
evaluate policy-generated reflections. In contrast, SCOPE internalizes
error localization and skill generation through supervised
initialization, enabling the policy to provide its own corrective
guidance during online RL. Compared with OPID, SCOPE improves ALFWorld
success by 13.4, 8.4, and 33.3 percentage points across the three
backbones. It also outperforms GRSD by 11.0 and 6.2 points on Qwen2.5-3B
and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively, while matching its ALFWorld success on
Qwen3-1.7B. These results support the effectiveness of self-bootstrapped
corrective guidance without external online analysis.

#### Selective step guidance versus trajectory-level skills

Compared with trajectory-level SEED, SCOPE improves ALFWorld success by
5.9 and 2.3 points on the Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B backbones,
respectively, while gaining 6.3 points on WebShop for both. On
Qwen3-1.7B, SCOPE ties GRSD at 92.2% ALFWorld success and exceeds SEED
and GRSD on WebShop success. Notably, SCOPE achieves the highest WebShop
success across all backbones without consistently leading in normalized
task score, suggesting stronger exact task completion rather than
uniformly better partial matches. These results are consistent with the
value of aligning distillation with selected error steps instead of
applying trajectory-level guidance broadly.

We further examine whether these improvements extend to a larger 32B
backbone in Section
[4.9](#S4.SS9 "4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.3 Diagnosing Trajectory-Level Supervision

To examine the limitations of trajectory-level supervision, we analyze
the alignment between task outcomes, step quality, and skill-conditioned
distillation signals. Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a)
reveals substantial outcome–step mismatch in annotated WebShop
trajectories: 29.8% of steps in successful trajectories are erroneous,
while 42.4% of steps in failed trajectories are correct. This
disagreement indicates that terminal outcomes alone cannot reliably
identify which decisions require correction.

Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(b)
further reveals that skill-unrelated steps account for 57.9% of nonzero
sampled-token teacher–student gaps. Notably, their negative and positive
gaps have similar magnitudes to those at skill-relevant steps
($`-0.378/+0.230`$ versus $`-0.400/+0.249`$ nats). This suggests that
gap magnitude alone provides limited information about the relevance of
corrective guidance. Together, these findings motivate explicit error
localization and selective error-step distillation, rather than applying
skill-conditioned supervision broadly. Detailed diagnostic protocols are
provided in Appendix
[B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Motivation Diagnostics ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

Figure 4: Training dynamics on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-3B. (A) Component
ablations. (B) Signed-gap slope $`\alpha`$. (C) Tanh saturation bound
$`c`$. (D) Pairwise length temperature $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$. The full
setting is $`\alpha=2.5`$, $`c=1`$, and $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}=0.1`$,
labeled All in (A) and by its parameter value in (B)–(D).
Trajectory-level guidance uses one skill per trajectory and distills all
steps. Lines connect observed checkpoints; the success axes start at 10%
in (A) and 40% in (B)–(D).

### 4.4 Ablation Studies

We evaluate six variants with Qwen2.5-3B on ALFWorld (Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"))
to examine the contributions of SCOPE’s components and different forms
of guidance. Together with the parameter sweeps in Section
[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Parameter Sensitivity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
these experiments also examine the effect of guidance strength. All
endpoint comparisons in this section use training step 180, where the
full configuration achieves 98.4% overall success.

Table 2: Ablation results on ALFWorld (%). Qwen2.5-3B at training step
180. We evaluate the effects of supervised initialization, skill
guidance, and length-reward design. Traj.-level guidance assigns one
skill per trajectory and distills across all steps; skill-bank guidance
uses retrieved skills. Overall success is micro-averaged across
evaluation episodes. Best values, including ties, are bold.

#### Supervised initialization supports subsequent self-analysis

Removing SFT initialization lowers overall success from 98.4% to 92.2%,
a 6.3-point drop. Its effect is also visible during training: at step
100, the full configuration reaches 96.1%, compared with 78.1% without
SFT (Figure
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Diagnosing Trajectory-Level Supervision ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(A)).
Heat is especially affected at the final checkpoint, falling from 100.0%
to 70.6%. These results highlight the need to first equip the model to
locate errors and generate corrective guidance before relying on its own
analyses for online supervision.

#### Matching skills to target steps improves guidance

Replacing step-specific skills and selective coverage with one skill per
trajectory and distillation over all steps reduces success to 96.1%, a
2.3-point drop. Replacing the generated guidance with skill-bank
guidance yields 95.3%, a 3.1-point drop. Together with the
unrelated-step signals in Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Diagnosing Trajectory-Level Supervision ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
these results support constructing guidance from the current trajectory
and restricting its application to the relevant decisions. The
trajectory-level variant changes skill granularity and coverage jointly,
so its result supports their design.

Figure 5: Interaction efficiency during training. Mean environment
interaction steps on ALFWorld across different training configurations.

#### Pairwise length rewards promote sustained efficiency

Removing the length reward reduces overall success from 98.4% to 93.0%,
while replacing the pairwise reward with an absolute length bonus yields
97.7%. Unlike absolute length shaping, our pairwise reward compares
successful trajectories within each on-policy group, adapting its
preferences as the policy improves. Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Matching skills to target steps improves guidance ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
shows that SCOPE rapidly reduces interaction steps during early training
and maintains low interaction counts in later stages, consistently
outperforming GRPO in efficiency. Compared with removing length rewards,
pairwise shaping generally maintains shorter trajectories after the
initial training phase. Together, these results support efficient task
completion without sacrificing success.

### 4.5 Training Dynamics

To examine learning efficiency and optimization stability, we compare
the training trajectories of SCOPE and GRPO and investigate the impact
of unbounded OPSD updates.

#### SCOPE reaches strong performance with fewer updates

Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c)
shows that SCOPE reaches 65.1% mean success on WebShop at step 60,
surpassing GRPO’s final 63.0% at step 150, requiring 60.0% fewer online
updates. On ALFWorld, SCOPE first exceeds GRPO’s final success rate of
76.6% at step 25, compared with step 145 for GRPO, reducing the required
updates by 82.8%. At step 180, SCOPE achieves 98.4% success, compared
with 76.6% at GRPO’s final checkpoint. These comparisons measure online
updates after supervised initialization, demonstrating faster
performance improvement under a smaller RL update budget.

#### Bounded signed distillation stabilizes training

Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c)
further shows that Unbounded SCOPE suffers an abrupt performance
collapse after initial improvement, whereas bounded SCOPE maintains
stable training. Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Bounding the signed learning signal ‣ 3.3 Bounded Signed Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reveals the underlying numerical instability: sharply reduced student
log-probabilities produce extreme teacher–student gaps, amplifying
raw-gap OPSD updates during minibatch optimization. The bounded signed
coefficient in Equation
[8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ Bounding the signed learning signal ‣ 3.3 Bounded Signed Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
limits this gap-driven amplification while preserving both positive and
negative corrections. Together, these results support stable and
efficient online optimization.

### 4.6 Parameter Sensitivity

![Refer to
caption](2610.38391v1/scope-parameter-sensitivity-compact.png)

Figure 6: Parameter sensitivity of SCOPE. Left: effects of gap slope
$`\alpha`$, saturation bound $`c`$, and pairwise temperature
$`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$ on task success. Right: task-wise performance
under different parameter settings, where Full denotes the default
configuration ($`\alpha=2.5`$, $`c=1`$, $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}=0.1`$).

To examine the sensitivity of corrective supervision and length-aware
optimization, we vary the signed-gap slope $`\alpha`$, saturation bound
$`c`$, and pairwise temperature $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$ individually.
The remaining parameters follow the default configuration
($`\alpha=2.5`$, $`c=1`$, $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}=0.1`$). Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.6 Parameter Sensitivity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reports overall and task-wise ALFWorld success at training step 180.

#### The signed-gap slope controls corrective strength

Reducing $`\alpha`$ to 1 lowers overall success from 98.4% to 89.8%,
with notable declines on Cool and Look. A smaller slope weakens the
coefficient for moderate teacher–student gaps, potentially limiting
corrective supervision. Increasing $`\alpha`$ to 5 maintains 97.7%
success, suggesting that effective learning does not depend on the exact
default slope.

#### Overly tight saturation limits correction

Reducing $`c`$ to 0.1 lowers overall success to 94.5%, with Heat
dropping to 82.4%. This suggests that early coefficient saturation can
restrict useful corrective updates. Both $`c=1`$ and $`c=10`$ achieve
98.4% overall success, indicating that SCOPE performs well across
different saturation bounds.

#### Moderate pairwise preferences favor performance

Setting $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$ to 0.05 or 0.2 yields 93.8% and 96.1%
success, respectively, compared with 98.4% at the default 0.1. Lower
temperatures produce sharper length preferences, while higher
temperatures soften pairwise differences. The intermediate setting
achieves the highest success in this sweep, supporting a balance between
length discrimination and corrective learning.

and SEED analyzers on WebShop and ALFWorld, evaluated using precision,
recall, F1, and parsing accuracy.

Figure 8: Unseen ALFWorld. Generalization to unseen instances across six

### 4.7 Error-Localization Capability

Since SCOPE relies on self-generated error analysis to select critical
steps, reliable error localization is essential for effective corrective
supervision. We therefore evaluate the localization capability of base
and SFT-initialized models on WebShop and ALFWorld, alongside a
SEED-style analyzer. Figure
[8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Moderate pairwise preferences favor performance ‣ 4.6 Parameter Sensitivity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reveals three key findings.

First, larger models generally exhibit stronger error-step localization,
with 7B outperforming 3B across most metrics. Second, SFT substantially
improves both backbones, with 3B SFT even surpassing 7B Base in
micro-F1, demonstrating that smaller models can acquire effective
error-analysis capabilities. Third, the SEED-style analyzer exhibits
markedly weaker localization than our step-specific analyzer,
particularly on ALFWorld, suggesting that trajectory-level hindsight
training may be less effective for fine-grained error identification.
These results support supervised initialization for reliable online
self-analysis. Metric definitions are provided in Appendix
[B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Error-Localization Evaluation Metrics ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.8 Generalization to Unseen Tasks

#### SCOPE generalizes to unseen task instances

To examine whether SCOPE transfers beyond the tasks encountered during
training, we evaluate its performance on the unseen ALFWorld split,
covering six household task families. As shown in Figure
[8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Moderate pairwise preferences favor performance ‣ 4.6 Parameter Sensitivity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
SCOPE achieves 89.6% overall success compared with 66.4% for GRPO, a
gain of 23.2 percentage points. Improvements span all six families,
particularly Look (+73.3 points), Pick2 (+50.0), and Cool (+32.4). These
results demonstrate that SCOPE’s learned corrective behavior generalizes
to unfamiliar task instances across diverse household routines.

#### Generalization gains accompany greater efficiency

Beyond higher task success, SCOPE also reduces average interactions from
18.86 to 10.06 turns, a 46.7% reduction relative to GRPO. This
improvement indicates that SCOPE generalizes without relying on longer
interaction sequences, achieving more successful completions with fewer
environment interactions. Together with the length-reward ablation,
these findings support the effectiveness of efficiency-aware agentic RL.

### 4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B

To investigate whether SCOPE remains effective at a larger model scale,
we extend our evaluation to Qwen3-32B on ALFWorld, covering both seen
and unseen task instances. We compare SCOPE against GRPO using the same
backbone. Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reports the results, while Figure
[9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
presents single-run training dynamics on the seen split.

Table 3: Qwen3-32B results on ALFWorld. Seen results are reported at
training step 150, while unseen evaluation covers 134 episodes.
Task-family and overall success rates are percentages; mean steps
measure environment interactions per episode. Best values within each
split are bold.

Figure 9: Training dynamics with Qwen3-32B. Single-run ALFWorld
seen-evaluation curves comparing SCOPE and GRPO across six task
families, overall success, and mean interaction steps. The dotted line
marks step 150, corresponding to the seen results in Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

#### SCOPE remains effective at larger model scale

At step 150, SCOPE achieves 99.2% overall success on Qwen3-32B,
outperforming GRPO (85.2%) by 14.0 percentage points. Improvements
extend across all six task families, with particularly large gains on
Pick2 (+30.0 points), Look (+25.0), and Cool (+19.2). These results
indicate that SCOPE’s targeted corrective supervision remains effective
when extended to a substantially larger Qwen3 backbone.

#### Higher success with fewer interactions

Figure
[9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 4.9 Scaling SCOPE to Qwen3-32B ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
shows that SCOPE improves rapidly during early training and maintains
near-ceiling success in later stages. On seen tasks, average
interactions decrease from 22.0 to 7.7, a 65.0% reduction. The gains
also extend to 134 unseen ALFWorld episodes, where SCOPE achieves 94.0%
success versus 81.3% for GRPO (+12.7 points), while reducing average
interactions by 47.2%. Together, these results demonstrate that SCOPE
retains both performance and efficiency advantages at larger model
scale, including on unseen tasks.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we identify two limitations of trajectory-level
supervision for LLM agents: trajectory outcomes obscure intermediate
decision quality, while trajectory-level skills can introduce off-target
distillation signals. To address these challenges, we propose SCOPE,
which internalizes error localization and applies self-generated,
step-specific corrective guidance only at selected error steps. Bounded
signed distillation controls gap-driven updates, while success-relative
pairwise rewards encourage efficient task completion. Experiments on
ALFWorld and WebShop across three backbones demonstrate consistent
improvements over outcome-based RL and strong performance against
skill-guided methods. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, SCOPE achieves 89.6%
success, outperforming GRPO by 23.2 percentage points while reducing
reported interactions by 46.7%. These results highlight the importance
of aligning corrective supervision with the decisions that require it,
without additional guidance at inference time.

## Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

We analyze three properties of SCOPE: bounded signed updates, the
influence of irrelevant distillation tokens, and the success-relative
length reward. The distillation results hold for a fixed training
microbatch and characterize its auxiliary update, not the convergence of
the full RL objective.

### A.1 Bounded Signed Distillation

Let $`\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{sel}}`$ be the selected token
set, with $`n=|\mathcal{I}|>0`$. For each token $`k\in\mathcal{I}`$,
define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle r_{k}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\ell_{k}^{T}-\ell_{k}^{S}(\theta),`$ |  | (16) |
|  | $`\displaystyle v_{k}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{k}^{S}(\theta),`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle f(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle=c\tanh(\alpha r/c),\quad\alpha,c>0.`$ |  |  |

We hold the sampled tokens, selected steps, and teacher scores fixed. As
in Equation
[8](#S3.E8 "Equation 8 ‣ Bounding the signed learning signal ‣ 3.3 Bounded Signed Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
gradients do not pass through $`f(r_{k})`$. The resulting auxiliary
gradient is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g(\theta)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}f(r_{k}(\theta))v_{k}(\theta).
``` |  | (17) |

For $`n=0`$, we define the auxiliary loss and gradient to be zero.

###### Proposition A.1 (Log-cosh gradient equivalence).

Define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\varphi(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{c^{2}}{\alpha}\log\cosh(\alpha r/c),`$ |  | (18) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Phi(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}\varphi(r_{k}(\theta)).`$ |  |  |

Then $`\nabla_{\theta}\Phi(\theta)=g(\theta)`$. The scalar potential
$`\varphi`$ is nonnegative, symmetric, and strictly convex, with its
unique minimum at $`r=0`$. Moreover,

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\varphi(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha}{2}r^{2}+O(r^{4}),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle r\to 0,`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\varphi(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle=c|r|-\frac{c^{2}}{\alpha}\log 2+o(1),`$ |  | $`\displaystyle|r|\to\infty.`$ |  |  |

###### Proof.

Differentiation gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\varphi^{\prime}(r)=f(r),\qquad\varphi^{\prime\prime}(r)=\frac{\alpha}{\cosh^{2}(\alpha r/c)}>0.
``` |  | (20) |

Since $`\ell_{k}^{T}`$ is fixed, $`\nabla_{\theta}r_{k}=-v_{k}`$. Thus
$`\nabla_{\theta}\Phi=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k}f(r_{k})v_{k}=g`$.
Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from $`\cosh x\geq 1`$ and
$`\cosh(-x)=\cosh x`$. Finally, the expansions
$`\log\cosh x=x^{2}/2+O(x^{4})`$ near zero and
$`\log\cosh x=|x|-\log 2+o(1)`$ at infinity give Equation
[19](#A1.E19 "Equation 19 ‣ Proposition A.1 (Log-cosh gradient equivalence). ‣ A.1 Bounded Signed Distillation ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
∎

This result interprets the detached distillation update as a log-cosh
gradient: small gaps receive approximately linear signed coefficients,
while large gaps have bounded influence.

###### Proposition A.2 (Bounded auxiliary gradient).

For any finite $`r`$,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|f(r)|`$ | $`\displaystyle<c,\qquad f(0)=0,`$ |  | (21) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\operatorname{sign}f(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{sign}r,`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle 0<f^{\prime}(r)`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\alpha.`$ |  |  |

If $`\|v_{k}\|\leq B_{k}`$ for each selected token, then

|     |                                                  |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \|g\|\leq\frac{c}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}B_{k}.
       ```                                               |     | (22) |

In particular, $`\|g\|\leq cB`$ when $`B_{k}\leq B`$ for all $`k`$.

###### Proof.

The coefficient bounds follow from the range and monotonicity of
$`\tanh`$, together with $`f^{\prime}(r)=\alpha/\cosh^{2}(\alpha r/c)`$.
By the triangle inequality,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\|g\|\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}|f(r_{k})|\|v_{k}\|\leq\frac{c}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}B_{k}.
``` |  |

∎

###### Corollary A.3 (Sensitivity to teacher scores).

Suppose the cached teacher score for token $`k`$ changes by $`e_{k}`$,
while the student and selected set remain fixed. If $`\|v_{k}\|\leq B`$,
the resulting gradient $`\widetilde{g}`$ satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\|\widetilde{g}-g\|\leq\frac{B}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}}\min\{\alpha|e_{k}|,2c\}.
``` |  | (23) |

###### Proof.

Since $`|f^{\prime}(r)|\leq\alpha`$ and $`|f(r)|<c`$,
$`|f(r+e)-f(r)|\leq\min\{\alpha|e|,2c\}`$. Substituting this bound into
Equation
[17](#A1.E17 "Equation 17 ‣ A.1 Bounded Signed Distillation ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and applying the triangle inequality proves the claim. ∎

Together, these bounds show that $`\alpha`$ controls local sensitivity
and $`c`$ limits gap-dependent amplification. They assume bounded token
score gradients and do not imply a global stability guarantee for RL
training.

### A.2 Influence of Irrelevant Selected Tokens

Step selection removes unselected tokens from the auxiliary loss. To
examine the effect of imperfect selection, partition
$`\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{rel}}\cup\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{off}}`$
into relevant and irrelevant selected tokens, and let
$`\eta_{\mathrm{off}}=|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{off}}|/n`$.

###### Proposition A.4 (Off-target gradient contribution).

Assume $`\|v_{k}\|\leq B`$. The gradient contribution from irrelevant
tokens,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{\mathrm{off}}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{off}}}f(r_{k})v_{k},
``` |  |

satisfies

|     |                                                 |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \|g_{\mathrm{off}}\|\leq cB\eta_{\mathrm{off}}.
       ```                                              |     | (24) |

If $`\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{rel}}\neq\varnothing`$, let
$`\overline{g}_{\mathrm{rel}}`$ be the mean auxiliary gradient over
relevant tokens alone. Then

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \|g-\overline{g}_{\mathrm{rel}}\|\leq 2cB\eta_{\mathrm{off}}.
       ```                                                            |     | (25) |

###### Proof.

Each token contributes a vector of norm at most $`cB`$ before
normalization, proving Equation
[24](#A1.E24 "Equation 24 ‣ Proposition A.4 (Off-target gradient contribution). ‣ A.2 Influence of Irrelevant Selected Tokens ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
Moreover,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g=(1-\eta_{\mathrm{off}})\overline{g}_{\mathrm{rel}}+g_{\mathrm{off}}.
``` |  |

Since $`\|\overline{g}_{\mathrm{rel}}\|\leq cB`$, the triangle
inequality gives
$`\|g-\overline{g}_{\mathrm{rel}}\|\leq\eta_{\mathrm{off}}cB+cB\eta_{\mathrm{off}}`$.
∎

Thus, reducing the fraction of irrelevant selected tokens tightens a
worst-case bound on their effect. This result quantifies the role of
selection but does not assume that the analyzer is always correct.

### A.3 Properties of Success-Relative Efficiency Rewards

Consider a task group with $`M=|\mathcal{S}_{q}|`$ successful
trajectories and positive interaction lengths $`T_{i}`$. The pairwise
score $`b_{i}`$ is defined in Equation
[11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ 3.4 Success-Relative Pairwise Efficiency ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

###### Proposition A.5 (Pairwise reward properties).

For $`M\geq 2`$ and $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}>0`$, the scores satisfy:

1.  (i)
    *Length ordering:* $`0<b_{i}<1`$, and $`T_{i}<T_{j}`$ implies
    $`b_{i}>b_{j}`$; equal lengths give equal scores.
2.  (ii)
    *Scale invariance:* replacing all $`T_{i}`$ with $`aT_{i}`$ for any
    $`a>0`$ leaves every $`b_{i}`$ unchanged.
3.  (iii)
    *Mean-bonus conservation:*

    |  |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{q}}b_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{M}{2},`$ |  | (26) |
    |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{q}}(R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}-R_{i})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}M}{2}.`$ |  |  |

The last identities also hold for $`M=1`$ and $`M=0`$ under the
conventions in Equation
[11](#S3.E11 "Equation 11 ‣ 3.4 Success-Relative Pairwise Efficiency ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

###### Proof.

For distinct successes $`i,j`$, Equation
[10](#S3.E10 "Equation 10 ‣ 3.4 Success-Relative Pairwise Efficiency ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
gives $`p_{ij}>p_{ji}`$ whenever $`T_{i}<T_{j}`$. The sigmoid is
strictly monotone, so $`p_{ik}>p_{jk}`$ for each other success $`k`$.
Hence

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle(M-1)(b_{i}-b_{j})={}`$ | $`\displaystyle p_{ij}-p_{ji}`$ |  | (27) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{q}\setminus\{i,j\}}(p_{ik}-p_{jk})>0.`$ |  |  |

Equal lengths give equality, and $`0<p_{ij}<1`$ implies $`0<b_{i}<1`$.
This proves (i). For (ii),
$`\log(aT_{j})-\log(aT_{i})=\log T_{j}-\log T_{i}`$. Finally,
$`p_{ij}+p_{ji}=1`$, so

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{q}}b_{i}=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{i<j}(p_{ij}+p_{ji})=\frac{M}{2}.
``` |  |

Multiplying by $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}`$ proves (iii). The cases
$`M=0,1`$ follow from the definitions. ∎

###### Corollary A.6 (Success–failure reward ordering).

If $`R_{i}\geq R_{j}`$ for every successful trajectory $`i`$ and failed
trajectory $`j`$, then for $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}>0`$,
$`R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}>R_{j}^{\mathrm{pair}}`$. Among successes with
equal original rewards, shorter trajectories receive larger shaped
rewards.

###### Proof.

For a success $`i`$, $`b_{i}>0`$, whereas a failure receives no length
bonus. Therefore,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{i}^{\mathrm{pair}}-R_{j}^{\mathrm{pair}}=(R_{i}-R_{j})+\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}b_{i}>0.
``` |  |

The ordering among equally rewarded successes follows from Proposition
[A.5](#A1.Thmscopeproposition5 "Proposition A.5 (Pairwise reward properties). ‣ A.3 Properties of Success-Relative Efficiency Rewards ‣ Appendix A Theoretical Analysis ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(i).
∎

The pairwise reward therefore favors shorter successes without a fixed
length target. Its mean bonus is always $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}/2`$
across successes, while the relative allocation changes with the current
rollout group.

## Appendix B Experimental Details

### B.1 Training Configuration

SCOPE follows the supervised-initialization and online-training workflow
of SEED \[[29](#bib.bib18)\]. Table
[4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.1 Training Configuration ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
summarizes the key coefficients used by the full method. The policy
snapshot supplies both the actor and the online analyzer; its
skill-conditioned teacher scores are cached before student optimization.
Online analysis has no separate supervised loss: the policy is updated
through the joint objective in Equation
[15](#S3.E15 "Equation 15 ‣ 3.5 Joint Policy Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
For the smaller backbones, training uses two NVIDIA H200 GPUs on WebShop
and four on ALFWorld. The Qwen3-32B experiments use 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

| Parameter                                             | Value |
|-------------------------------------------------------|-------|
| Maximum skill entries $`K_{\max}`$                    | 5     |
| Signed-gap slope $`\alpha`$                           | 2.5   |
| Saturation bound $`c`$                                | 1     |
| Distillation weight $`\lambda`$                       | 0.01  |
| Length-preference temperature $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$ | 0.1   |
| Length-bonus weight $`\lambda_{\mathrm{len}}`$        | 5     |
| PPO clipping radius $`\epsilon`$                      | 0.2   |
| Reference KL weight $`\beta_{\mathrm{ref}}`$          | 0.01  |
| Entropy weight $`\lambda_{H}`$                        | 0.001 |

Table 4: Key settings of full SCOPE. Parameter sweeps vary one of
$`\alpha`$, $`c`$, or $`\tau_{\mathrm{len}}`$ at a time.

The main comparison uses the step-150 checkpoint. ALFWorld ablations and
parameter sweeps use step 180. Training-step savings in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c)
compare the first observed checkpoints reaching GRPO’s final mean
success rate.

### B.2 Validation Curves Across Backbones

To complement the multi-seed training dynamics in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c),
we report single-run validation curves for SCOPE with
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld and WebShop.
Both figures mark training step 150, the checkpoint used for the main
comparison in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

Figure 10: Single-run validation curves on ALFWorld. Overall and
task-family success rates, together with mean environment interaction
steps, for SCOPE-3B and SCOPE-7B. The dotted vertical line indicates
step 150, whose overall success rates match Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

Figure 11: Single-run validation curves on WebShop. Success rate,
normalized task score, and mean environment interaction steps for
SCOPE-3B and SCOPE-7B. The dotted vertical line indicates step 150; the
success rates and normalized scores match Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

As shown in Figures
[10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ B.2 Validation Curves Across Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and
[11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.2 Validation Curves Across Backbones ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
both backbones improve substantially during online training while
reducing interaction steps. At step 150, SCOPE-3B and SCOPE-7B reach
97.7% and 98.4% overall ALFWorld success, respectively. On WebShop, they
achieve 85.2% and 84.4% success, with normalized task scores of 87.9%
and 89.6%, respectively. The corresponding mean interaction counts are
8.24 and 7.73 on ALFWorld, and 6.02 and 5.95 on WebShop. These results
provide single-run training context for the main-table checkpoint
values.

### B.3 Supervised Data and Hindsight Analysis

GLM-5.2 generates the offline annotations used for SFT. Each input
contains the task description, episode outcome, and the recorded
sequence of observations and responses, together with action-validity
feedback when available. Successful trajectories are analyzed for
avoidable errors. Failed trajectories may additionally receive up to
three successful action sequences from the same task as reference
context. These offline references can come from separate runs of that
task; online references are drawn from the current on-policy group.

The annotation configuration uses temperature 0, an output limit of
8,192 tokens, and disabled thinking. Observations are retained without
character-level truncation. An annotation contains a trajectory summary
and at most five skill entries, each with target-step indices, an error
explanation, and a short reusable corrective instruction. Entries that
require the same correction can cover multiple steps. The prompt asks
the annotator to judge decisions using the information available at each
step and to preserve reasonable exploration. An empty skill list is
returned when no clear error is supported.

The data pipeline checks the JSON structure, nonempty required fields,
and valid, unique target indices before export. Each SFT example is a
system–user–assistant conversation: the input is the analysis prompt,
and the assistant target contains only the structured summary and skill
entries. Successful reference action lists remain in the input rather
than in the prediction target. The same analysis instructions and output
schema are used by the online analyzer, which is the current policy
snapshot. If a failed group contains no success, the reference block is
omitted and the analyzer judges the recorded trajectory directly.
Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C SFT and Analyzer Prompt Templates ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
provides the templates.

### B.4 Error-Localization Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate error-step localization against reference annotations. For
each trajectory $`i`$, let $`E_{i}`$ and $`\widehat{E}_{i}`$ denote the
reference and predicted error-step sets, respectively. Predictions are
extracted from the target_steps fields of generated skill entries.

#### Step-level metrics

Micro-precision and micro-recall are defined as
$`P=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}`$ and
$`R=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}`$, with counts
aggregated across all trajectories. Micro-F1 is $`\frac{2PR}{P+R}`$,
while Macro-F1 averages the F1 scores computed separately for each
trajectory.

#### Trajectory-level metrics

Exact Match measures the fraction of trajectories with
$`\widehat{E}_{i}=E_{i}`$. Parse Rate measures the fraction of outputs
satisfying the required JSON schema. All metrics are reported as
percentages.

### B.5 Motivation Diagnostics

#### Outcome–step mismatch

The WebShop study in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ SCOPE: Selective Critical-Step On-Policy Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a)
uses GLM-5.3 to identify erroneous steps in 1,400 trajectories: 536
successful and 864 failed episodes. Local decision quality is judged
separately from episode outcome: an eventual success can contain
avoidable mistakes, and an eventual failure can contain correct
decisions. The figure reports error and correct-step proportions
separately for the two outcome groups. GLM-5.2 supplies the offline SFT
annotations described above; GLM-5.3 supplies these diagnostic
error-step labels.

#### Off-target probability shifts

The skill-influence analysis scores 33,602 steps and 4,035,655 response
tokens from 177 task groups. The recorded relevance labels divide steps
into 14,081 related and 19,521 unrelated steps according to the
applicability of the trajectory-level skill. On the sampled response
tokens, we compute the signed gap
$`\Delta=\log\pi_{T}(y\mid h,s)-\log\pi_{S}(y\mid h)`$. Within each
outcome and relevance group, positive and negative bars are pooled-token
means conditional on $`\Delta>0`$ and $`\Delta<0`$, respectively. Zero
gaps are excluded from these conditional means. The 57.9% off-target
share divides the number of nonzero-gap tokens at unrelated steps by the
number of nonzero-gap tokens at all steps. The negative and positive
shares of 53.9% and 46.1% use nonzero-gap tokens at unrelated steps as
their denominator.

Error bars show 95% task-group bootstrap intervals from 2,000 resamples
with random seed 0. Task descriptions and initial observations define
the grouping proxy; each resample draws complete groups rather than
individual tokens. This preserves within-group dependence when
estimating uncertainty in the conditional means.
````
